title: NASA's Roman Telescope Is Cleared to Launch
hook: Hubble sees deep; Roman is built to see wide. NASA has cleared its next flagship observatory for a late-August launch to map cosmic expansion across huge swathes of sky.
key_points: NASA reports the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has passed its final pre-launch review.
Liftoff is targeted for August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy.
Its science goals: cosmic expansion, the history of the universe, and distant exoplanets.
Roman's edge is survey speed — a very wide field of view at space-telescope sharpness.
Wide surveys are how you test dark energy: you need millions of galaxies, not a few deep stares.
content_html: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has been cleared for final launch preparations, with liftoff targeted for August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. It is the agency's next big astrophysics observatory, and its mission is to probe how the universe is expanding, how it got to look the way it does, and what distant planetary systems are made of.
extra_html: Roman's distinguishing feature isn't depth — it's width. Hubble and JWST are built to stare hard at small patches of sky; Roman is built to sweep across large ones at comparable sharpness. That matters because the biggest open questions in cosmology are statistical. Whether dark energy is a true constant or something that evolves, and how dark matter is laid out across the cosmic web, are questions you answer by measuring the positions, shapes and distances of enormous numbers of galaxies at once. The same wide, repeated imaging also catches brief microlensing flickers — the tell-tale brightening when one star drifts in front of another and a planet's gravity nudges the light — which is how Roman is expected to add to the exoplanet census. Launch dates slip, so treat August 30 as a target rather than a promise.

related.title: Is Dark Energy Changing Over Time?
related.hook: For decades dark energy looked like a constant. New galaxy-survey data hints it may evolve — and that would shift even our measured value of the cosmic expansion rate.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: The Expanding Universe
related.hook: Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees — not because they're moving through space, but because space itself is stretching.

related.title: Dark Energy Survives a Major Challenge
related.hook: A bold claim said the universe's accelerating expansion was an illusion. Astronomers checked the math, found the mistakes — and cosmic acceleration came out as strong as ever.

flashcards.prompt: What capability sets Roman apart from Hubble?

choices.text: A far wider field of view, so it can survey large areas of sky quickly
Much sharper images of single objects than any telescope before it
The ability to observe from the ground as well as from orbit

flashcards.explanation_html: Roman is a survey instrument. Its advantage is breadth of sky per exposure, not a deeper stare at one target — which is what dark-energy cosmology needs.

flashcards.prompt: Why does studying dark energy require a wide-field survey telescope?
flashcards.back_html: Dark energy is measured statistically — from how millions of galaxies are distributed and how fast they recede. That demands mapping huge areas of sky, not observing a handful of targets.

flashcards.prompt: What are Roman's headline science targets?
flashcards.back_html: Cosmic expansion, the history of the universe, and distant exoplanets — one observatory aimed at both the largest scales and individual worlds.
